Every leaf on Earth is running the same trade. It opens tiny pores to let carbon
dioxide in, and water walks out through the same doorway. How well a plant does that
trade — how much sugar it gets per litre of water — decides where it can live.

The three tools below build that picture one piece at a time. The first has no pores
at all, and no water: just the chemistry, with you supplying the CO₂. The second adds
the pores, and with them the cost. The third watches three completely different
solutions play out over a whole day.

Everything runs in your browser. Move a slider and the answer is recomputed on the
spot — nothing is fetched, so it works on a bad connection and keeps working with the
network off.

## 1. What limits a leaf?

A leaf builds sugar with three things: an enzyme called **Rubisco** that grabs CO₂,
**light energy** to power the reaction, and somewhere to **put the sugar** once it is
made. At any moment one of those three is the bottleneck, and which one it is changes
as the day and the seasons change.

For now, forget about the pores. Imagine you can dial the CO₂ concentration *inside*
the leaf directly, and watch what the chemistry does.

::: {.ph-tool}
::: {.ph-controls #ph-limits-controls}
:::
::: {.ph-chart #ph-limits-chart}
:::
::: {.ph-readout #ph-limits-readout}
:::
:::

The heavy red line is what the leaf actually achieves. The three faint dashed lines
behind it are the three ceilings — enzyme, light, sugar export — and the leaf is always
held down by the lowest one. Notice that the red line does not follow the lowest ceiling
exactly but rounds the corner where two of them cross: near a changeover, *both*
processes are partly limiting at once.

::: {.ph-try}
Things to try

- **Halve the Rubisco capacity.** The flat part of the curve drops a long way, but the
  steep part near zero light barely moves. That early slope is set by photons, not
  enzyme — which is exactly why a leaf growing in deep shade should not waste nitrogen
  building Rubisco it will never use.
- **Now halve the electron-transport ratio instead.** This time the slope moves and the
  plateau holds. Two different knobs, two different parts of the curve.
- **Switch to the CO₂ tab** and watch where the enzyme and light ceilings cross as you
  change the light. That crossing *is* the changeover, and it slides.
- **Set the internal CO₂ to 150 ppm**, roughly a leaf with its pores nearly shut, then
  to 400, wide open. You have just previewed the whole of Section 2.
- **Push the temperature to 40 °C.** Everything collapses — but look at the respiration
  number, which is still climbing. Heat costs a leaf twice.
:::

You have been setting the internal CO₂ by hand. A real leaf cannot do that. To let CO₂
in it has to open its pores, and the moment it does, water starts leaving.

## 2. The price of carbon is water

Now the pores are in the model. You set the CO₂ in the **air**; the leaf decides how far
to open, and therefore what its internal CO₂ becomes — the number you were dialling
yourself a moment ago.

Opening wider buys more carbon and costs more water. How bad that bargain is depends on
how *thirsty the air is*: the drier the air, the more water escapes through the same
opening. And warm air is thirsty air, because warm air can hold far more water vapour.

::: {.ph-tool}
::: {.ph-controls #ph-water-controls}
:::
::: {.ph-chart #ph-water-chart}
:::
::: {.ph-readout #ph-water-readout}
:::
:::

::: {.ph-try}
Things to try

- **Keep humidity fixed and sweep the temperature.** Carbon peaks around 25 °C. Water
  keeps climbing to about 30 °C. And the ratio between them — the bottom strip — falls
  the whole way, by roughly five-fold from a cool morning to a hot afternoon.
- **Now switch to "dryness of the air stays the same."** The ratio goes almost flat.
  That is the whole lesson in one click: the temperature penalty on water-use efficiency
  is not the enzymes giving up, it is the *air* getting greedier. A plant cannot
  acclimate its way out of that one.
- **Raise the CO₂ in the air to 800 ppm.** Efficiency goes up *and* water use goes down —
  the leaf can get what it needs without opening as far.
- **Halve g₁** to make a cautious, drought-adapted leaf, and read off what that caution
  costs in carbon.
- **Watch "CO₂ inside ÷ outside"** as you change the light and the CO₂. It barely moves.
  Leaves hold that ratio remarkably steady, and what sets it is not light or CO₂ but how
  dry the air is.
:::

Every leaf so far has been a C3 leaf — the ordinary kind, and about 85 % of plant
species. If the price of carbon is water, are there other ways to pay it?

## 3. Three ways to pay that price

There are, and plants found two of them.

**C4** plants run a CO₂ pump. They spend extra energy concentrating CO₂ around Rubisco,
which lets them keep their pores tighter for the same carbon gain. Maize, sugarcane and
most tropical grasses do this.

**CAM** plants go further and simply move the whole operation to the night. They open
their pores in the cool, damp dark, stash the CO₂ as an acid, seal up at dawn, and spend
the day making sugar from yesterday's air. Cacti and agaves do this.

Watch all three over one simulated day, and read what each one gained and spent.

::: {.ph-tool}
::: {.ph-controls #ph-pathways-controls}
:::
::: {.ph-chart #ph-pathways-chart}
:::
::: {.ph-budget-host #ph-pathways-budget}
:::
:::

::: {.ph-caveat}
**A word about the CAM line.** The C3 and C4 curves come from the same research model
the rest of this page uses. The CAM curve does not — it is a deliberately simple sketch,
because a real CAM plant runs on a daily internal clock that this page does not try to
simulate. It captures the parts that matter here: pores open at night, shut by day, and
a hard ceiling set by how much acid last night's storage could hold. It leaves out the
dawn and dusk windows when real CAM plants do take in some CO₂ directly.

The flat daytime line means *no exchange with the air* — not "nothing happening." Inside
the leaf, sugar is being made at full speed.

One more caution: the efficiency numbers here are for **one leaf on one day**. Textbooks
often quote CAM as three to ten times more water-efficient than C3, but those are
whole-plant, whole-season figures that include CAM plants shutting down entirely for
months. This page cannot show that, and does not pretend to.
:::

::: {.ph-try}
Things to try

- **Follow a single C3 day.** Light peaks at noon. But carbon peaks in the *mid-morning*,
  a couple of hours earlier, and water use peaks later still. Ask yourself why the leaf's
  best hour is not the sunniest one.
- **Compare mid-morning with mid-afternoon** at the same light. The afternoon gets less
  carbon for more water. Section 2 already told you why: the air has warmed up and dried
  out, even though the sun has not changed.
- **Click "Hot desert."** The C3 leaf loses about 70 % of the carbon it got in Ithaca.
  CAM loses barely any. CAM is not the most *efficient* pathway in the desert — it is the
  one that hardly notices the desert.
- **Look at C4's water column in that desert.** It uses *more* water than the C3 leaf,
  while being more efficient per unit. Efficiency is not the same as thrift, and that
  distinction matters when the water runs out.
- **Click "Wet tropics."** CAM's efficiency advantage is at its largest here — and its
  point is at its smallest. Nobody needs it where it rains every afternoon. Now ask where
  CAM plants actually grow.
- **Open the "Response to light" tab** and find where the C3 and C4 curves cross. Below
  that light level, the ordinary C3 leaf wins. Then move the temperature and watch the
  crossing move.
:::

## What the model is doing

::: {.ph-howto}

**Three ceilings, and the lowest one wins.** The enzyme ceiling depends on how much
Rubisco there is and how much CO₂ reaches it. The light ceiling depends on how many
photons arrive. The export ceiling is a fixed rate at which the leaf can ship sugar out.
Near a changeover both are partly limiting, so the model rounds the corner rather than
switching abruptly.

**Photorespiration is why CO₂ matters so much.** Rubisco sometimes grabs oxygen instead
of carbon dioxide, and the leaf has to spend energy cleaning up the mistake. The lower
the CO₂ inside the leaf, the more often it happens — which is why the curve in Section 1
does not start at zero, and why raising CO₂ helps a C3 leaf so much. C4 and CAM plants
have both found ways to concentrate CO₂ around Rubisco and largely avoid it.

**Warm is good until it isn't.** Enzymes speed up with temperature, then start to come
apart. Every rate in the model rises to an optimum and falls past it, which is why the
curves peak. Respiration keeps rising longer than photosynthesis does, so a hot leaf is
squeezed from both ends.

**Stomata are doing arithmetic.** The model asks what opening gets the most carbon for
the least water, given how dry the air is. It turns out the answer keeps the internal
CO₂ at a nearly constant *fraction* of the outside air — which is why that number barely
moves in Section 2 no matter what else you change.

**What this page simplifies.** The leaf is assumed to be the same temperature as the air
and the air is assumed to be well stirred. A real leaf in still, bright sun runs several
degrees hotter than the air, which pushes it further along every curve here. There is
also no soil in this model, so no plant on this page can ever run out of water — worth
remembering when you click "Hot desert."

:::

## Where this comes from

**Start here.** If you want to read further, these two are written to be read:

- **von Caemmerer, S. (2000).** *Biochemical Models of Leaf Photosynthesis.* CSIRO
  Publishing. The book-length version of everything on this page.
- **Lambers, H. & Oliveira, R.S. (2019).** *Plant Physiological Ecology*, 3rd ed.,
  chapter 2. Covers C3, C4 and CAM and the water trade-off at about the level of
  Sections 2 and 3.

**The model itself.** The equations behind Sections 1–3, and the papers they come from:

- Farquhar, G.D., von Caemmerer, S. & Berry, J.A. (1980). A biochemical model of
  photosynthetic CO₂ assimilation in leaves of C3 species. *Planta* 149:78–90.
  **Section 1 is this paper.**
- Collatz, G.J., Ribas-Carbo, M. & Berry, J.A. (1992). Coupled photosynthesis–stomatal
  conductance model for leaves of C4 plants. *Australian Journal of Plant Physiology*
  19:519–538. **The C4 pathway in Section 3.**
- Medlyn, B.E. et al. (2011). Reconciling the optimal and empirical approaches to
  modelling stomatal conductance. *Global Change Biology* 17:2134–2144. **The pores, and
  therefore all of Section 2.**
- Bernacchi, C.J. et al. (2001). Improved temperature response functions for models of
  Rubisco-limited photosynthesis. *Plant, Cell & Environment* 24:253–259.
- Medlyn, B.E. et al. (2002). Temperature response of parameters of a biochemically
  based model of photosynthesis. *Plant, Cell & Environment* 25:1167–1179. **Why the
  curves fall past their optimum.**
- Bolton, D. (1980). The computation of equivalent potential temperature. *Monthly
  Weather Review* 108:1046–1053. The saturation vapour pressure formula behind every
  humidity number here.

**For the pathways in Section 3:**

- Ehleringer, J. & Björkman, O. (1977). Quantum yields for CO₂ uptake in C3 and C4
  plants. *Plant Physiology* 59:86–90. **The measurement behind the C3/C4 crossover in
  dim light and cool temperatures.**
- Sage, R.F., Sage, T.L. & Kocacinar, F. (2012). Photorespiration and the evolution of
  C4 photosynthesis. *Annual Review of Plant Biology* 63:19–47.
- Osmond, C.B. (1978). Crassulacean acid metabolism: a curiosity in context. *Annual
  Review of Plant Physiology* 29:379–414.
- Nobel, P.S. (1991). *Physicochemical and Environmental Plant Physiology*; and Lüttge,
  U. (2004). Ecophysiology of crassulacean acid metabolism. *Annals of Botany*
  93:629–652. The CAM acid-storage numbers behind the sketch in Section 3.

### How this model actually works

The leaf model on this page is the same one used by **MEDS**, the lab's ecosystem model.
If you want the equations in full — including the parts this page leaves out, like the
leaf boundary layer, plant hydraulics, and how drought closes stomata — see
[Leaf gas exchange](https://github.com/xiangtaoxu/MEDS/blob/v0.1.0/docs/science/leaf_gas_exchange.md)
in the MEDS science documentation.

The numbers here are pinned to
[MEDS v0.1.0](https://github.com/xiangtaoxu/MEDS/releases/tag/v0.1.0), and the JavaScript
in this page is checked against the model's own Fortran code case by case, so the curves
you are moving are the ones the research model produces.

Xu, X. and the BioM2 Lab (2026). *MEDS: a Fortran 2018 reimplementation of the Ecosystem
Demography model*, v0.1.0.
